q: what's the difference between the swing desk and the day desk?
a: Kestrel splits its money into two desks, 50% each, and judges them separately so a losing one can't hide behind a winner. The swing desk holds stocks for days to weeks and decides once a day at 3:45pm New York time, 15 minutes before the close. It can hold up to 8 positions of at most 12.5% of its money, with a 7% stop-loss. The day desk is in and out the same day: it decides every 5 minutes, holds at most 3 positions of up to 33% each, makes no new trades in the last 30 minutes and sells everything 10 minutes before the close. A ticker can only be on one desk.
source: trader/config.yaml (desks.swing, desks.day); trader/aitrader/engine.py (module docstring, desk_orders); trader/aitrader/config.py (check_config)

q: swing desk vs day desk, how are they different
a: Think of them as two separate traders sharing the account. The swing desk is the patient one: it looks at daily prices, makes one decision a day 15 minutes before the close (3:45pm ET on a normal day), and keeps positions for days or weeks. It spreads its half of the money over as many as 8 stocks, 12.5% each, and sells anything that falls 7% below its buy price. The day desk watches 5-minute prices, can hold 3 positions of up to 33%, and never keeps anything overnight. Each desk goes through study, paper and real money on its own.

q: when does the swing desk actually make its trades?
a: Once a day, 15 minutes before the close: 3:45pm New York time on a normal day, 12:45pm on early-close days. That's when it scores its stocks and places buys and sells. The rest of the trading day the autopilot still checks the swing positions every 5 minutes, but only for stop-losses. It decides near the close because its backtest decides and fills at each day's close, and the same code runs in testing, paper and live, so what was tested is what trades.
source: trader/run.py (due_jobs: swing and swing-stops jobs); trader/aitrader/engine.py (module docstring); trader/aitrader/market_hours.py (session_close)

q: how many stocks can the swing desk hold at once
a: Up to 8, each at most 12.5% of the swing desk's money. With the default $1,000 of paper money the swing desk gets $500, so a full position is about $62. It also keeps a 1% cash buffer. If one stock grows to more than twice its share (over 25% of the desk), it's trimmed back to 12.5%. Each position has a 7% stop-loss.
source: trader/config.yaml (desks.swing.risk, paper.starting_cash, desks.swing.budget_pct); trader/aitrader/risk.py (position_size, trim_qty, TRIM_AT)

q: why does the swing desk hold 8 stocks and not 3?
a: It used to be 3. In the bot's own backtest from 2011 to 2026, momentum with 8 to 10 holdings traded about 3 times as often as with 3, made about the same, and had a smaller worst drop: roughly -42% to -47% instead of -57%. Spreading over more stocks also means each position is smaller (12.5% of the desk), so one bad stock hurts less. It's a backtest result, not a guarantee, but it's why the setting is 8.

q: whats the stop loss on swing trades
a: 7%: if a swing position falls 7% below what it paid, it's sold. During market hours the bot checks this every 5 minutes, and when trading in a broker account it also leaves a stop order resting at the broker, so a sleeping or crashed laptop can't stop the sale. One honest limit: a stop can't sell overnight. If a stock gaps down at the open (after earnings, say), it sells at the next open, wherever that is, which can be worse than 7%.

q: how does the day desk work?
a: The day desk trades 5-minute prices and is always out by the close. During market hours it decides every 5 minutes. It can hold up to 3 positions, each up to 33% of its money (often less, because each trade's risk is capped). It opens no new trades in the last 30 minutes and sells everything 10 minutes before the close. If it ever finds a position left over from an earlier day (for example the laptop was asleep), it sells it first. Its list is a fixed watchlist plus up to 10 'stocks in play' picked each morning at 9:35.

q: does the day desk ever hold overnight?
a: No. Ten minutes before the close it sells everything, with the reason 'end of day: day trades are never held overnight'. And if a position somehow survives to the next day, for example because the Mac was asleep at the close, the very next cycle sells it before doing anything else. That's also why the day desk doesn't need the earnings check the swing desk uses: it's never holding when a report comes out after hours.

q: what time does the day desk stop trading
a: On a normal day the market closes at 4:00pm New York time. The day desk opens no new trades from 3:30pm (30 minutes before the close) and sells everything at 3:50pm (10 minutes before). On early-close days, when the market shuts at 1:00pm, those become 12:30pm and 12:50pm. Stop-losses keep working right up to the sell-off.

q: how much money does each desk get?
a: Each desk gets 50% of the total. With the default $1,000 of paper money, that's $500 for the swing desk and $500 for the day desk. Real money works the same way off the real-money cap you set in Setup: with a $50 cap, each desk would get $25. The bot never borrows and never uses more than that cap, whatever else is in the account.

q: can the same stock be on both desks?
a: No, a ticker can be on only one desk. The settings check refuses a stock listed on both watchlists. The daily scan also skips the day desk's stocks when picking for the swing desk, and the morning stocks-in-play check skips anything the swing desk watches, considers or holds. Separately, it skips stocks you own yourself in a shared account, to keep your shares apart from the bot's.

q: what are the phases kestrel goes through?
a: Each desk moves on its own through four steps. Study: at least 30 calendar days and 20 trading days of watching, with no real orders; meanwhile it trades 'in its head' with pretend money. Plan review: it backtests every method, adds the study results and writes a plan, which may honestly say don't trade. Paper: you approve the plan and it trades fake money, in Alpaca's paper account or simulated on the Mac. Live: only if the paper results pass every rule and you confirm. A kill switch on a live desk sends it back to paper.

q: what does 'in its head' mean
a: While a desk is still studying, it also trades with pretend money simulated on your Mac, using the same rules as paper trading: same stops, sizes and limits. The swing desk practices momentum and the day desk practices TJR's model. Every pretend trade and each day's result shows in the app's Trades tab, next to the paper and real-money accounts. If the pretend account trips the kill switch, it sells (in pretend), notes it, and carries on. Mistakes made in its head still count for the mistake memory.

q: which strategy is the day desk practicing right now?
a: In its head, the day desk practices TJR's model (tjr_model), set in config.yaml under study.in_its_head_strategy; the swing desk practices momentum. The day desk's study still shadow-trades all its methods side by side (opening range breakout, the 5-minute ORB, VWAP reversion, the AI and TJR's model), so it can compare them. TJR's model only moves to paper trading after its weekly history test passes and you start Stage 2.

q: what happens during the study month
a: No real orders. Every trading day after the close it studies. On the swing desk, every method writes down an opinion on every stock with the price, and 5 trading days later it grades each opinion against what really happened. On the day desk, every method is shadow-traded on that day's real 5-minute prices with fake money, under the same rules as paper trading. It needs at least 30 calendar days and 20 trading days of this. Because the decisions are made before the outcome is known, it's an honest report card, though a small one.

q: how does it pick which strategy to trade after studying?
a: It backtests every method on all the history it has and checks the study month. To be picked, a method needs a Sharpe of at least 0.5, a profit factor of 1.15 or more, a worst drop no bigger than 25% and at least 30 backtest trades. On top of that, swing needs 10+ graded buy opinions with a positive edge; day needs 10+ shadow trades that made money. Of the ones that pass, it picks the best Sharpe. If none pass, the plan says NO_TRADE and the desk keeps studying. You still have to approve the plan.

q: when will kestrel trade real money?
a: Only when three things are all true. First, the desk earned it: after at least 30 trading days of paper trading it made money, beat simply holding SPY over the same days, and never dropped more than 10% from its best day. Second, LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED=true is set on the Mac and it has real-time prices. Third, you type the confirmation (REAL MONEY) yourself. There's no minimum trade count right now, because momentum trades rarely.

q: how does a desk go from paper to live
a: It runs the promotion check, desk by desk. The rules: at least 30 trading days of paper trading, a total return above 0%, a worst drop of no more than 10%, and a return better than SPY's over the same period. The closed-trade count and profit factor checks are blank in config.yaml, so they're off for now. If everything passes, it still needs real-time prices, LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED=true in the Mac's settings, and you typing REAL MONEY. Nothing goes live automatically.

q: whats the plan? stage 1, stage 2 etc
a: Stage 1: the swing desk paper trades the momentum method for 30 trading days, skipping the study month. Stage 2: once TJR's model passes its weekly history test on the Mac's own 5-minute data, you start it on the day desk, also in paper, for 30 trading days, while Stage 1 keeps running. After that, real money: about $50 at Alpaca first (Schwab is also planned, with $50). Real money still needs the paper results to pass and your typed confirmation.
source: trader/aitrader/knowledge/20-the-plan.md; trader/aitrader/knowledge/10-safety-rules.md (fractional shares: the $50 test starts at Alpaca); trader/run.py (start_stage1, start_stage2)

q: what is stage 1
a: Stage 1 is the swing desk paper trading the momentum method with pretend money for 30 trading days. You start it with Start Stage 1 paper trading in Setup (or python run.py start-stage1, typing YES). It skips the study month for the swing desk; the day desk keeps studying. There's no backtest run for it on the Mac; it rests on the 16-year research. To pass it has to make money, beat SPY over the same days and not drop more than 10% from its best day.

q: what's stage 2
a: Stage 2 adds TJR's model on the day desk, in paper trading, next to Stage 1 on the swing desk. It can't start until the model passes its history test, which the autopilot runs about once a week on the Mac's own 5-minute data: 30+ trades, a profit factor of at least 1.15, making money, and a better profit factor than random buys with the same stop and target. Then you press Start Stage 2 in Setup. It only enters trades from 9:35 to 11:30am and sells everything before the close.

q: can i start stage 2 now?
a: Only if TJR's model has passed its history test. If it hasn't, Start Stage 2 refuses and tells you which part failed, such as too few trades (it needs 30) or no better than random entries. The test runs after a close about once a week, and needs the day desk's 5-minute history. Stage 2 also can't start if the day desk is already paper trading or is on real money. Until then the day desk keeps practicing TJR's model in its head.

q: will 30 days of paper trading prove the strategy works?
a: No, and the bot says so itself. Thirty trading days can catch a broken method, but can't prove a good one. In the 16-year research, even the best method made money and beat SPY in only about 6 of 10 30-day windows (58%), and momentum with the trend filter about half the time (49%). So passing is a reason to try small real money, and failing isn't always proof it's bad. That's why the first real-money test is planned at about $50.

q: how much real money is it going to use
a: The plan is small: about $50 at Alpaca first, with $50 at Schwab also planned and Webull possibly later. More only if it makes money. The cap is a setting in Setup (the most real money the bot may use), and the bot never spends more than it or borrows, whatever else is in the account. The money is split 50/50 between the desks, so a $50 cap means $25 per desk.

q: how does momentum work
a: Momentum is Stage 1's method on the swing desk. It ranks every stock on its list (the watchlist plus the 30 strongest stocks from the daily scan that it can afford) by its return over the last 12 months, skipping the most recent month. It buys from the top 20% as long as the stock is above its 200-day average. It sells when a stock drops out of the top half of the ranking or falls below its 200-day average. While the S&P 500 (SPY) is below its own 200-day average, it buys nothing new but keeps what it owns.

q: how does the swing desk decide what to buy
a: Right now (Stage 1) it uses momentum. At 3:45pm it lines up every stock it's considering, its watchlist plus up to 30 strong, affordable names from the daily scan, and ranks them by how much they rose over the past 12 months, leaving out the latest month. A stock in the top 20% that's also above its 200-day average is a buy, strongest first, while there are free slots (8 in total) and cash. If SPY itself is under its 200-day average, it holds what it has and buys nothing new.

q: why momentum? does it actually work
a: It was the one stock-picking method with real-world support in the 16-year research. The bot's test numbers for it are flattered, because the stock list only holds today's survivors. The honest yardstick is a real momentum fund, MTUM, which made about 16% a year since 2013 against 14.4% for SPY. So the realistic expectation is the market plus a point or two a year, with bigger drops. The bot's old swing rules made only 0.7-1.6% a year and aren't used.

q: why did the swing desk sell something
a: One of four things: the 7% stop-loss was hit; momentum's score fell below 0.5, meaning the stock dropped out of the top half of its ranking; the stock fell below its 200-day average (its score goes to 0); or it was a trim because one stock grew to more than twice its 12.5% share. Every sale has its reason written next to it in the Activity list and the journal, so you can see which one it was. The market falling below its 200-day average doesn't force sales; it just stops new buys.

q: why isn't it buying anything?
a: Several rules can stop new buys, and the after-market report lists the reason under its thinking. Common ones: all slots are full (8 swing, 3 day); SPY is below its 200-day average (momentum then buys nothing new); the desk is down more than 3% today; a strong stock has danger news or, on the swing desk, an earnings report within 3 trading days; the Risk agent is skipping a repeated mistake; the strategy has been paused by its own lessons; or it's the day desk's last 30 minutes. Sometimes nothing simply scores high enough.
source: trader/aitrader/engine.py (decide_orders, desk_orders, run_cycle, remember_thinking); trader/aitrader/strategies.py (Momentum); trader/run.py (_trade_desk, earnings_hold, learned)

q: what's trend_following
a: A swing method the bot compares during its study. It rides uptrends: it buys when the price is above its 50-day average and the 50-day average is above the 200-day average, and it sells when the price falls below the 50-day average. It isn't the Stage 1 method; it would only be traded if it won the plan review after a study month.

q: what does mean_reversion do
a: It's a swing method that buys sharp short-term dips in stocks that are still in a long uptrend: the 2-day RSI drops under 10 while the price is above its 200-day average. It sells on the bounce, when the price closes above its 5-day average. It's one of the methods compared during the study. The research found RSI-2 dip buying lagged simply holding SPY, so it has a high bar to clear.

q: what's ai_swing
a: It's the swing desk's machine-learning model, running on your own Mac (gradient-boosted decision trees). For each stock it estimates the chance the price is higher in 5 trading days. It buys when that's at least 56% and sells when it drops below 48%. It re-learns about once a month (every 21 trading days) and isn't trusted until it has about 2 years (500 days) to learn from. It only ever learns from the past, so its backtest isn't cheating.

q: what's opening_range_breakout
a: A day-desk method. The first 30 minutes after the open set the day's opening range, and it has no opinion while that range forms. After that, it buys if the price breaks above the range's high and exits if the price falls back below the middle of the range. Like every day trade, anything still open is sold 10 minutes before the close.

q: whats orb_5min and how is it different from the normal opening range breakout
a: orb_5min is the research version, long only. The first 5 minutes set the range, not 30. If that first 5-minute candle closed up, it buys when the price breaks above its high. It sells if the price falls 10% of the stock's usual daily range (14-day ATR) below that high; otherwise it holds to the end of the day. One try per stock a day. In the study it came from, it worked on stocks in play and not on random stocks, and a 30-minute range did much worse.

q: what's vwap_reversion
a: A day-desk method that buys dips below the day's average traded price (VWAP). It buys when the price is more than 0.5% below VWAP and looks oversold (14-bar RSI under 30), and sells when the price gets back to VWAP. It skips the first 15 minutes of the day, which are the most chaotic. It's one of the day methods the bot compares in shadow trades.

q: what's ai_day
a: The day desk's local machine-learning model. Every 5 minutes it estimates the chance a stock is higher in an hour (12 five-minute bars, never past today's close). It buys at 55% or more and sells below 48%. It re-learns about once a week and needs about 20 trading days of 5-minute history before it starts. It learns only from the past. It's compared with the other day methods during the study.

q: whats tjr's model
a: It's the setup from TJR's trading videos, coded for the day desk, long only. It only buys while the stock's hourly trend is up. It waits for price to dip below a low where stop orders sit (yesterday's low or a recent 5-minute swing low), which is the 'sweep'. Then a 5-minute bar has to close above the last swing high. It buys when price pulls back into the gap that move left, between 9:35 and 11:30am. The stop goes just below the sweep, the target is twice the risk, and it's one trade per stock a day.

q: explain tjr strategy in simple terms
a: The idea: big moves often start with a fake-out. Price drops just below an obvious low, which triggers other traders' stop-losses, then turns around and breaks back up. Kestrel waits for that whole sequence on 5-minute bars: hourly trend up, a dip below yesterday's low or a recent swing low, then a close above the last swing high. It buys on the pullback into the price gap the move left, only from 9:35 to 11:30am, with a stop just under the dip and a target of 2 times the risk.

q: what exactly are the rules in tjr.py
a: Bias: the latest confirmed hourly swing low is higher than the one before, and the last hourly close is above it. Sweep: a bar trades below yesterday's low or a 5-minute swing low. Break: within 12 bars, a 5-minute close above the last swing high before the sweep. Gap: the bullish gap that move left, at least 0.05% of the price. Entry: within 12 bars, a bar dips into the gap and doesn't close through it, between 9:35 and 11:30am. Stop: the sweep's low minus a quarter of the 5-minute ATR. Target: 2R. One trade per stock a day, long only.

q: how does tjr's model exit a trade
a: The model scores 0 once its own stop (below the sweep's low, minus a quarter of the 5-minute ATR) or its target (2 times the risk) is reached, and the day desk sells at that 5-minute check. On top of that, the day desk's normal stop-loss still applies, and everything is sold 10 minutes before the close no matter what. So a trade ends at the stop, the target or the end of the day, whichever comes first.
source: trader/aitrader/tjr.py (docstring: scores for the engine, ticker_scores); trader/aitrader/engine.py (decide_orders, desk_orders)

q: what's the tjr history test?
a: It's the gate before TJR's model may paper trade. About once a week, after the close, the autopilot replays the model on the Mac's own 5-minute history using the day desk's real rules: slots, position sizes and costs. It passes only with at least 30 trades, a profit factor of 1.15 or better, a profit, and a better profit factor than a placebo that buys at random moments in the same 9:35-11:30 window with the same stop and target. The result is in the journal and in Setup.
source: trader/aitrader/tjr.py (history_test, PASS, TJRPlacebo); trader/run.py (run_tjr_test, TJR_TEST_EVERY_DAYS, due_jobs)

q: why compare tjr with random trades
a: Because a stop and a 2-to-1 target can look profitable on their own. The placebo buys at random moments in the same 9:35-11:30am window, with the same trend filter, stop and target, so if TJR's setup can't beat it per trade, the setup itself isn't adding anything. That was a real concern: in the 16-year daily test, TJR longs averaged +0.24R per trade, but random entries with the same stop and target got +0.18R.
source: trader/aitrader/tjr.py (TJRPlacebo, ticker_scores placebo branch, history_test); trader/aitrader/knowledge/30-research-findings.md (TJR's model on daily charts)

q: has tjr's model actually been proven to work?
a: Not yet. From his videos so far (50 of 200 analyzed) there are 55 recorded trades, but none verified by fills or broker statements, so they're claims. On 16 years of daily charts, the long setup made only a little more than random entries and the edge shrank after 2018; as an account it made 13.1% a year against 14.4% for SPY. His real method is intraday on futures, so the bot tests it on its own 5-minute stock data. Even a pass means 'worth paper trading', not proof.

q: does kestrel short stocks
a: No. Every method only buys and later sells what it owns; it never bets on a stock falling. TJR's model is coded long only on purpose: shorting it lost in every version of the 16-year test (-0.24R per trade on daily charts), and the bot doesn't short. It also never borrows money.

q: why did it buy NIO
a: NIO is on the day desk's fixed watchlist, so any buy came from the day desk's method. Every buy carries its reason, like the method's name and 'score 1.00 >= 0.9', in the Activity list and the journal, and the after-market report shows what it traded, why, and the team's notes on that decision. If the desk was practicing TJR's model, a score of 1.0 means the full setup happened: hourly trend up, a sweep, a break above the swing high and a pullback into the gap. Check the journal entry for that day for the exact reason.

q: what's the daily all-stocks scan
a: After each close (around 4:20pm New York time), the autopilot looks at every tradable US stock and ETF from Alpaca, or about 400 popular names without Alpaca keys. It drops anything under $3 a share or trading less than $5 million a day on average. It ranks the rest by 12-month momentum (skipping the latest month) and keeps only uptrends: above the 200-day average, with the 50-day above the 200-day. The top 30 make the list. Newly listed stocks get a separate watch-only list of 5. It also reads the news.

q: how does the swing desk use the scan?
a: Every day it adds the 30 strongest stocks from the scan that it can afford to its own watchlist, never the day desk's stocks. With fractional shares any price fits; with whole shares, only stocks where one share fits in a position. Momentum then ranks all of them together and buys from the top 20%, so it can own strong stocks you never listed. The scan only proposes; the desk's rules and budget still decide every trade.

q: it bought a stock thats not on my swing watchlist, why?
a: That's by design. The swing desk's list is the watchlist in config.yaml plus the 30 strongest stocks from the daily all-stocks scan that it can afford. The scan ranks every US stock by its 12-month rise (skipping the latest month) and keeps only uptrends. Momentum then ranks the whole combined list, so a strong stock from the scan can beat the watchlist names. You can see the scan list under Research & plans, 'Stocks it likes'.

q: what happens if the scan fails
a: The scan runs in the background so trading never waits for it. If it fails (the Mac slept, an update restarted it, or Alpaca refused too many requests), it tries again in 5 minutes, up to 3 times. If the list is still old the next morning, it scans again then, so the 3:45pm swing decision picks from fresh results. The after-market report says when the list was last made, or why not.

q: what's danger news
a: When news is on, the bot reads recent headlines (the last 3 days) from Alpaca's news feed, or Yahoo without keys. If a stock's headlines contain words like offering, bankrupt, chapter 11, trading halt, delist, going concern, SEC charges, fraud, reverse split, default, restatement or subpoena, it won't buy that stock for now. Stocks in play with danger news are skipped too. News never makes it buy anything; it only keeps it away.
source: trader/aitrader/scanner.py (DANGER_WORDS, danger, danger_tickers); trader/config.yaml (news); trader/run.py (_trade_desk); trader/aitrader/in_play.py (run)

q: what are stocks in play
a: Stocks that are trading far more than usual right at the open, often because of news, earnings or big buyers. At 9:35am New York time the bot compares each busy stock's volume from 9:30 to 9:35 with its average for those same 5 minutes over the last 14 days. That ratio is relative volume. The top 10 at 1.0x or more join the day desk's list for that day only. The fixed watchlist stays, so a failed check never leaves the desk with nothing to trade.

q: why is the day desk trading a stock that isn't on its watchlist?
a: It was probably one of that morning's stocks in play. Each day at 9:35am the bot adds up to 10 stocks with unusually heavy trading in their first 5 minutes to the day desk's list, for that day only. They come from a pool of the busiest stocks in the evening scan: $5+ a share, 1 million+ shares a day, and a usual daily move of at least $0.50. Stocks with danger news or that belong to the swing desk are left out. The journal lists each day's picks with their relative volume.

q: does trading stocks in play actually help?
a: The research says it can: a 2024 study of about 7,000 US stocks found the 5-minute opening-range breakout made +3.2% a year on all stocks but +41.6% on the top 20 by relative volume. But those numbers were tuned on the same data, used long and short trades with 4x borrowed money, no slippage and tight stops. So Kestrel tests it itself: the report splits day trades into 'in play' and 'fixed list', so its own results show whether in-play stocks help.

q: how is relative volume worked out
a: Relative volume is the shares traded from 9:30 to 9:35 today divided by the average for that same 5-minute window over the last 14 days. A stock needs at least 5 past days to be judged. It uses Alpaca's free IEX feed for both today and the past, so it compares like with like. IEX is only about 2.5% of all trading, which is fine for a ratio. It needs Alpaca keys; without them the day desk just uses its watchlist.

q: who are the agents on the team
a: Every decision goes through five agents, each with one job and a short note. Scout gathers the facts: scores, holdings, cash, danger news, option gaps and today's stocks in play. Analyst gives a view per stock: what agrees and what conflicts. Trader lists the orders from the desk's tested strategy. Risk checks every buy: its size, stocks that move together, option bets against it, and repeated mistakes. Reviewer grades the day after the close and passes on the lessons. The notes show in the after-market report.
source: trader/aitrader/agents.py (docstring, scout, analyst, trader, risk, reviewer); trader/aitrader/knowledge/35-team-and-options-gap.md

q: does the risk agent block trades?
a: Mostly it just warns. It checks every buy, notes when a stock moves closely with one the desk already owns (correlation 0.85 or higher), and lets the buy through, because the list of checks it may act on (risk_vetoes) is empty by default. The exception is repeated mistakes: it does skip a buy that would repeat a mistake the desk already made, and says why. It can only ever skip a buy, never add one, and it never blocks a sale.

q: what are risk vetoes, should i turn them on?
a: They're the checks the Risk agent may act on instead of just warning. There are two: 'correlation' skips a buy that moves with a stock already owned (correlation of 0.85+ over the last 60 days on swing, 60 five-minute bars on day), and 'options_gap' skips a buy when option bets lean against it. Both are off by default. The options one is only meant to be switched on once the options-gap watcher's scorecard shows an edge. A veto can only make it more careful.

q: does an AI chatbot decide the trades?
a: No. Trades come only from coded rules that were tested on history and then paper-traded. The 'AI' strategies are small machine-learning models on your Mac, scored like any other method. The local language model only writes plain-English explanations: the plan, the report summary, and some agent notes. A chatbot can't be backtested honestly, because it has read the news about the very years it would be tested on.

q: does it learn from its own trades?
a: Yes. After every finished trade it reviews which strategy bought it, how it ended, and what the market was like then: S&P 500 above or below its 200-day average, and calm or wild. Under 12 finished trades nothing changes. With 12+ trades and a losing average, that strategy trades at half size. Clearly losing over 30+ trades, it's paused. If its trades in one market condition clearly lost over 20+ trades, it makes no new buys while that condition holds. It never gets bolder after a winning streak.
source: trader/aitrader/learning.py (docstring, review, adjust, LEARNING_TRADES, PAUSE_TRADES, CONDITION_TRADES); trader/run.py (learned)

q: why is my strategy on half size
a: Because it's been losing so far. Once a strategy has at least 12 finished trades in that account and its average result is below zero, the bot halves its maximum position size: on the swing desk, 12.5% becomes 6.25% of the desk. It's re-checked after every trade, so once the average turns positive it goes back to normal. If it keeps losing clearly over 30+ trades, it gets paused instead.
source: trader/aitrader/learning.py (review, LEARNING_TRADES, PRIOR_TRADES); trader/run.py (learned: max_position_pct * size)

q: what does paused mean for a strategy
a: A strategy is paused when it has lost over at least 30 finished trades, with a negative average that's clearly below zero (at least 1 standard error), not just bad luck. While paused it opens no new trades, and the journal says why, but stop-losses and sales still work. Like every lesson, it's re-checked after each finished trade, so it can come off the pause if results change.

q: what are the market conditions it avoids
a: Each trade is tagged with the market at the time: the S&P 500 above or below its 200-day average, and calm or wild (its 20-day swings compared with their usual level). If the desk's trades in one condition have clearly lost money over at least 20 trades, and did worse than its trades overall, it makes no new buys while that condition holds. The reason shows in the journal, e.g. no new buys today because its trades in a wild market clearly lost.

q: what is the mistake memory
a: The owner's rule: making a mistake is fine; making the same one twice isn't. Every buy is saved with its situation as tags, like the stock itself, a stock under $5, chasing, or bought in the first 30 minutes. When a situation keeps losing in the last 60 days, it becomes a lesson, and the Risk agent skips new buys in that situation and says why. Lessons come from every account the desk traded (in its head, paper and real), only ever make it more careful, and never block a sale.

q: will it keep buying a stock that keeps losing?
a: Not for long. If the same stock has 3 or more finished trades in the last 60 days, at most 1 of them won, and they lost money overall, it becomes a lesson ('buying NIO', say). The Risk agent then skips new buys of that stock and writes the reason: the number of trades in the last 60 days, how many won, and the loss. Any stop-losses or sales still happen. The lesson fades once those trades are older than 60 days, unless it's confirmed again.

q: what tags does it record on a buy
a: The stock itself ('buying NIO'). A stock under $5. On the day desk: whether it was a stock in play or from the fixed list, and whether it was bought in the first 30 minutes or after 2pm. Chasing: on the day desk, already up 3% or more since the open; on the swing desk, up 10% or more in 5 days. Moving with a stock it already owns. And option bets against it. These tags are what the mistake memory groups trades by.

q: how many losses before a situation becomes a lesson
a: It depends on the kind. For a single stock: 3 or more trades in the last 60 days, at most 1 won, and losing money overall. For any other situation (chasing, first 30 minutes, under $5 and so on): 8 or more trades in the last 60 days, losing on average, worse than the desk's trades overall, and clearly so, at least 1 standard error below zero. The thresholds are small on purpose: the owner prefers learning fast to waiting for proof.
source: trader/aitrader/mistakes.py (find, STOCK_TRADES, SITUATION_TRADES, CLEARLY, WINDOW_DAYS); trader/aitrader/knowledge/37-mistakes.md

q: what's the relapse rule
a: Lessons fade after 60 days unless they're confirmed again, so the bot can notice when things change. But it remembers which lessons it learned. If a faded lesson's situation loses again later, the lesson comes back at once, without needing another 3 or 8 losing trades. The reason reads like 'lost again (ticker on date) after it had learned this once'.

q: do the lessons last forever
a: No. Both kinds of lessons are built to change. Mistake lessons only count the last 60 days, so they fade unless the same mistake keeps happening (a relapse brings one back right away). Strategy lessons (half size, paused, conditions to avoid) are recalculated after every finished trade, so a wrong one goes away by itself. A fixed rule would stop the bot from ever learning that things changed.

q: how are stops set on the day desk
a: Each stock gets its own stop, sized to how much it usually moves: half its usual daily range (the 14-day average true range, from earlier days only), kept between 1% and 5% below the buy price. If the range isn't known, it uses a fixed 2%. A position keeps the stop it was bought with, at the broker too. The swing desk doesn't do this; it keeps the fixed 7% stop it was tested with.

q: why do some day trades have wider stops than others?
a: Because a jumpy stock needs more room than a calm one, or normal wiggles would knock it out. The stop is half the stock's usual daily range, between 1% and 5%. The catch is that a wider stop buys a smaller position, so no trade risks more than 0.66% of the desk at its stop. That's what a full 33% position with a 2% stop used to risk. It's a common rule of thumb, not a proven edge, and the bot's own results will show whether it helps.

q: how big is a day trade?
a: Up to 33% of the day desk's money, but also small enough that hitting the stop loses no more than 0.66% of the desk. So the stop size sets the position. With $500: a 2% stop allows the full 33% (about $165); a 4% stop allows about 16.5% (about $82); a 1% stop is still capped at 33%. Either way the loss at the stop stays around $3.30 or less. It also keeps 1% of cash aside.

q: why did it sell only part of a position
a: That's a trim. If one stock grows to more than twice its allowed share of the desk, the bot sells it back down to the limit. On the swing desk that means a stock worth over 25% of the desk is trimmed back to 12.5%. The reason line starts with 'trim:' and shows the stock's share of the desk and the limit. It keeps the rest of the position; it only stops one stock from dominating.

q: what's the earnings check
a: The swing desk doesn't buy a stock whose next earnings report is within 3 trading days, today included. A report can move a stock 10-20% overnight, past the 7% stop, because a stop can't sell in the middle of the night. Dates come from Yahoo Finance, looked up each morning. Stocks it already owns are kept. Stocks with no known date, like ETFs, are never held back. The day desk doesn't need it because it never holds overnight.

q: will it sell a stock before its earnings report?
a: No. The earnings check only stops new swing buys within 3 trading days of a report. What the swing desk already owns is kept, and its stop still protects it, except that a report after hours can gap the price past the stop. That's a deliberate trade-off: on average stocks have actually done slightly better around earnings (over 7% a year in one study, smaller in later work), so skipping them is a safety choice, not a money-making one.

q: can i turn off the earnings check
a: Yes. It's in Setup, Settings: 'Don't buy right before earnings (swing desk)'. It's on by default with a 3-trading-day window. If the date lookup fails on a given day, the bot logs it and buys without that check that day rather than stopping the decision. Turning it off means more swing buys, but also more exposure to overnight surprises.

q: does it buy fractional shares?
a: Where the orders go can handle them: Alpaca (paper and real money) and the simulation on your Mac. It buys down to 0.0001 of a share, at least $1 at a time, and only for stocks Alpaca allows. Schwab's API trades whole shares only, and Webull's fractional orders aren't confirmed, so both get whole shares. A swing position's overnight resting stop at Alpaca covers only its whole shares; the bot watches the fraction itself every 5 minutes. You can switch fractional shares off in Setup.
source: trader/config.yaml (fractional); trader/aitrader/config.py (fractional_allowed); trader/aitrader/risk.py (floor_shares, MIN_ORDER_VALUE); trader/aitrader/brokers/live.py (docstring, stop_qty)

q: can it buy expensive stocks with such a small account?
a: With fractional shares (Alpaca or the simulation), yes, any price: it just buys part of a share. With whole shares (Schwab, Webull, or fractional switched off), a stock is skipped if one share costs more than a position's budget. With $500 per desk, that's about $62 a share on the swing desk (12.5%) and about $163 on the day desk (33%). With a $50 real-money test at Schwab, only cheap stocks would fit; the plan starts the $50 test at Alpaca, which can buy fractions.

q: what's the options gap watcher
a: A test that watches and grades, and never trades. After each close it looks at each watched stock's options (Alpaca's free data, expirations in the next 45 days): what share of the volume was calls, compared with that stock's normal share and its price over the last 5 days. A bullish gap is calls unusually heavy while the price hasn't risen; a bearish gap is puts unusually heavy while the price holds up. Each gap is graded 5 trading days later against SPY. The scorecard is in the after-market report.

q: does the options watcher affect trades?
a: Not by default. It's testing only. The Risk agent mentions a bearish gap in its note ('puts are piling up against it'), but only skips a buy if you add options_gap to the risk vetoes, and the intended rule is to do that only once the scorecard shows an edge: 20+ graded calls, right 55% of the time or more, with a positive average. Research is mixed: buyers' bets predicted next-week returns in one study, but public volume can't tell buyers from sellers.

q: what's the daily loss limit
a: Each desk has one: if the desk's value is more than 3% below where it ended yesterday, it makes no new buys for the rest of the day. It doesn't sell anything because of it; stop-losses, exits and the day desk's end-of-day sell-off keep working as normal. The next day it starts fresh.

q: what's the kill switch
a: If a desk's value falls 15% below its best point, the kill switch trips. In paper or real money it's an emergency stop: it cancels the bot's orders, sells everything that desk owns, and halts it until you resume. A desk trading real money also drops back to paper and has to earn real money again. In its head (pretend money) it sells the pretend positions, notes it and carries on.
source: trader/config.yaml (desks.*.risk.max_drawdown_pct); trader/aitrader/risk.py (kill_switch_tripped); trader/run.py (_trade_desk, emergency_stop, finish_if_flat); trader/aitrader/phases.py (docstring)

q: what happens if the account drops a lot
a: There are layers. Each position has a stop-loss: 7% on the swing desk, 1-5% sized to the stock on the day desk. If a desk is down more than 3% on the day, it stops buying for that day. If it falls 15% below its best point, the kill switch sells everything that desk owns and halts it, and a real-money desk drops back to paper. Separately, a desk can't go live at all if its paper trading ever dropped more than 10% from its best day.

q: what's the difference between pause and emergency stop
a: Pause means no new trades, but nothing is sold: stop-losses keep protecting what it owns, and the day desk still sells before the close. Emergency stop is for when you want out: you type SELL EVERYTHING (in the app, or /kill SELL EVERYTHING on Telegram), it cancels the bot's orders, sells everything it bought (never your own stocks) and halts both desks until you resume. Pausing from the phone is /pause.

q: what does the autopilot do every day
a: It wakes every 5 minutes on weekdays (New York time). 9:25am: check-in, login warnings, earnings dates, and a re-scan if the stock list is stale. 9:35am: stocks in play. During market hours: the day desk decides every 5 minutes and the swing desk checks its stops. 3:30pm: no new day trades. 3:45pm: the swing decision. 3:50pm: the day desk sells out. 4:10pm: the study. 4:15pm: the options watcher and the weekly TJR test. 4:20pm: the all-stocks scan. 4:25pm: the after-market report.

q: what does kestrel do after the market closes
a: About 10 minutes after the close it runs the study: grading swing opinions, shadow-trading the day methods, checking that live positions have stops resting at the broker, and writing one journal line per account. Five minutes later the options-gap watcher runs, plus TJR's history test if a week has passed. At 20 minutes it starts the all-stocks scan and news in the background, and at about 25 minutes it writes the after-market report.
source: trader/run.py (due_jobs, run_job: study, options, tjr, scan, report; protect_live; report_days)

q: what if my mac was asleep at 3:45
a: Then the swing desk misses that day's decision, and after the close the journal warns that it missed it. Positions in a broker account are still protected by stop orders resting at the broker. The day desk's resting stops expire that night, and any day position left over is sold at its first cycle the next morning. That's why the bot only works properly while the Mac is awake, online and plugged in.
